newsitem.title: USA: N.Y. jury weighs case of tennis star's death.
newsitem.headline: N.Y. jury weighs case of tennis star's death.

text.p: A jury began deliberating on Wednesday in the trial of a pool mechanic charged in the gas poisoning death of tennis star Vitas Gerulaitis.

Bartholomew Torpey and his employer East End Pools and Courts Inc. were accused of improperly installing an exhaust pipe in a Southampton, Long Island, pool cottage where Gerulaitis was a guest and died on Sept. 18, 1994, at age 40.
The jury deliberated three-and-a-half hours before recessing for the day. The panel also asked the judge to re-read the details of the charges in the case.

Torpey, indicted on charges of criminally negligent homicide, allegedly rigged an incorrect length of pipe from a pool heating system, trapping carbon monoxide gas near the room where the tennis player rested.
The pool company was charged with second-degree manslaughter.
In closing arguments on Wednesday, Torpey's defence attorney said the wrong man was being blamed for the tennis star's death.

Defence attorney John O'Brien argued that the pool heating manufacturer Teledyne Laars and its expert James Cosmano were aware the heater was improperly installed when Cosmano checked it three days before Gerulaitis died and did nothing about it.
"The District Attorney is offering you Bart Torpey as a sacrificial lamb," O'Brien told the Suffolk County jury. "I'm asking you not to be a party to that slaughter."

He added: "But for the actions of James Cosmano, Vitas Gerulaitis would still be playing tennis today. It was not Bart's actions or omissions, it was James Cosmano tinkering with the machine on Sept. 15."
Prosecutor Edward Heilig told the jurors the defence argument was a "mud defence" and an attempt to distract them.
"The issue is what happened, what caused it and could it have been prevented," Heilig told the jurors.

Gerulaitis, who retired from the tennis circuit in 1984 but later returned to the game as a broadcaster and played in exhibition matches, won 27 singles and nine doubles championships, including the 1977 Australian Open. He won millions of dollars but his career declined rapidly as he was treated for drug abuse.

Gerulaitis' mother, Aldona Gerulaitis, has filed a $63 million civil lawsuit in Manhattan Supreme Court, citing nine defendants, including Torpey, the pool company and Martin Raynes, the friend who owned the estate where Gerulaitis died.
